headline: Researchers from Rutgers University and IBM have shown that a 100-qubit IBM quantum processor can check and reset its own qubits mid-calculation, tipping from chaos into a controllable state at a sharp threshold.
score_reason: Pool 4 lowered by 1: the paper and release came out on 9 Oct 2026, before the 11 Oct window, and the result is a physics step, not a working fault-tolerant machine.
importance_line: What changed is that a real quantum processor carried out measurement-and-reset steps thousands of times in one run, a skill needed for error-corrected quantum computers, which matters first to quantum scientists and later to anyone waiting for useful quantum machines, but it is a step toward, not yet, a fault-tolerant computer.
summary: Rutgers University reports that its physicists, working with IBM and other institutions, ran an experiment on an IBM Quantum Heron processor, using a chain of up to 100 of its 156 qubits (the basic units of quantum computing), in which the machine alternated between scrambling information and repeatedly measuring and resetting qubits, nearly 5,000 times each, in a study published in Nature Physics and announced on 9 Oct 2026. The system switched abruptly from chaotic to controllable behaviour near an even split between the two steps, matching theory and showing the real-time feedback that error-correcting quantum computers will need, though Rutgers calls it a step toward a fault-tolerant machine, not the machine itself.
